processing: Heated to stop oxidation, then rolled and dried, as with other green teas; individual estates differ and some use orthodox methods.
harvest_season: Java's tropical highland gardens are not tied to a single famous spring picking the way Chinese and Japanese gardens are, and no particular season is documented as the prized one.
appearance_dry: Dark, twisted green leaf, varying a lot by estate.
appearance_wet: Green leaf of medium size, varying by estate.
taste_profile: Varies by estate; the highland tea from Ciwidey near Bandung is described as full-bodied and grassy.

brewing.notes: A general green-tea starting point, brewed Western-style. Taste after two minutes and adjust for the estate.

vintage_note: There is no vintage culture around this tea. It is sold by estate and grade rather than by year, and as with any green tea, freshness is what counts, so look for a recent packing date.
description:
Java green tea means green tea grown on the Indonesian island of Java, nearly always in the western highlands. It is a place name rather than one defined style, which is the first thing to know before buying.

Indonesia is mainly a black tea country, and green tea is the smaller side of it. West Java accounts for most of the national tea crop, around 69% in 2020 figures, so that is where the green tea comes from too.

The cups vary. A Ciwidey estate tea near Bandung is sold as full-bodied and grassy, while West Java's Chakra Dewata estate has reportedly moved past greens once thought too smoky. Brew in cooler water first, since the style of the estate decides what you will get.

Buy by estate name and ask for a packing date. Part of Java's small-scale green tea has traditionally gone into local jasmine tea, so scented tea is often what you will meet in Indonesia itself.
history:
Tea in Indonesia is mainly a black tea story, with green tea made in smaller amounts for local drinking. Commercial green tea production in West Java is reported to date only from the 1980s, though this rests on limited evidence.

Indonesian tea output has drifted down from around 160 thousand tons in 2000 to about 120 thousand in the 2020s, and some Java estates have since invested in improving their greens.
sources_note: Read from search snippets. The Ciwidey attribution and 1980s date are single-source.
